This is game 88 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (128,337 bytes)
- count.py (828 bytes)
- libs.py (1,378 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

The top group still needs eyes, so I'm thinking about which interior points to secure to make it alive, while also checking how black's C8 group interacts with that space.

Playing out options like F7, D8, or B8, I keep landing on small liberty counts for my groups, so none of these moves clearly resolve the shortage of eyes. I'm shifting to rough territory counting — black holds a large chunk on the right side while my area is mostly along the bottom — to gauge whether the overall position still favors me despite the local weaknesses.

Thinking through the left-side capturing race, my chain at B4/B5/C5 is actually safe since it connects into the big bottom group, but black's B6/C6/B7/C8 cluster has too many liberties to kill outright. That means my real priority has to be securing life for my top group first, and D8 looks like the move that both extends liberties and splits black's position.

Checking variations after D8 though, my top group's eye space still feels cramped and could end up with only two liberties if black plays D8 themselves to connect C8 — so I keep circling back to D8 as the best practical choice despite the risk.

Maybe instead I should try killing black's left group so my top group gets that area as eye space — tracing through B8, A7, A6 exchanges, but the liberty races keep cutting both ways and black seems to escape capture each time.

Stepping back, I think a simpler path is D8 then black B8; my top group would still have four liberties but faces continued pressure from F7. Black's left group in the corner has room for its own eyes, so this could turn into a genuine life-and-death race between the two groups rather than a clean kill.

Tracing it further: black plays E7 after D8, putting my top group in atari with only F7 left, but I capture the B6,C6,B7 group with A6, which reconnects liberties to my C7 group and lets the top survive — though this sequence feels too deep for a 12k-level engine to find. events.text:
I lost game 88 against the 12k opponent, playing White. I resigned at move 42 after my 9-stone top group was left with no way to make two eyes.

- **Opening:** I played C3 and C7 against Black's G7 and G3. That pair was too thin: once Black had E5 and D4, it pushed through at C4, C6 and B6. My C7 stone was cut off into a separate top group.
- **Middle game:** My attacks with D6, E6, F6 and F4 worked tactically, since Black had to answer G5. But the top group never got room for eyes.
- **Decisive mistake:** At move 28 I played B8, a wedge between Black stones with only two liberties. Black's A8 put it in atari, and Black then took B9 and C9, which was the top-left edge where my second eye had to be. Enclosing the top edge with E8 or F8 first would have given the group room to live.
- **End:** The group had one real eye at E7. The space at D9–E9 had Black stones at both ends, so Black could fill E9 and then E7. My last tries at G8 and G9 didn't change that.

I added this game to `CLAUDE.md`: the full move list, what went wrong, and a new lesson (#-32): a group squeezed between two enemy corners must secure its edge eye space before starting attacks elsewhere. The plan for next time as White against a G7/G3 opening is C3 + C6 instead of C7, keeping the left side as one group. My record as White against 12k is now 9 wins, 23 losses and 3 draws.
